INLA-style posterior approximation for any log-posterior

Source: R/inla-vanilla.R
inla_vanilla.Rd

Approximates the posterior of a parameter vector from its log density alone, using the approximation pipeline of INLAvaan with no latent field and nothing model-specific. The pipeline has four stages:

  1. Joint Gaussian (Laplace). The posterior mode \(\vartheta^*\) and the inverse Hessian \(\Omega\) there give a Gaussian approximation \(N(\vartheta^*, \Omega)\) and the Laplace estimate of the log marginal likelihood.

  2. VB mean correction. The Gaussian is recentred at \(\tilde\vartheta = \vartheta^* + \hat\delta\), the mean that maximises its expected log-posterior, with the covariance unchanged.

  3. Skew-normal marginals. For each parameter, the log-posterior is scanned along the conditional mode path of the Gaussian, corrected for the changing volume of the other parameters, and fitted by a skew-normal \(SN(\hat\xi_j, \hat\omega_j, \hat\alpha_j)\).

  4. Gaussian copula draws. sampling() couples the skew-normal marginals through the correlations of \(\Omega\).

Stages 2 and 3 are optional and independent of each other. vb = FALSE skips the VB correction, which leaves the marginals unchanged (they are scanned around the mode) but gives the Laplace log marginal likelihood. marginals = "gaussian" skips the scans and uses the Gaussian's own marginals \(N(\tilde\vartheta_j, \Omega_{jj})\), centred at the VB mean (or at the mode when vb = FALSE); sampling() then draws from the joint Gaussian. So vb = FALSE, marginals = "gaussian" is the Laplace approximation alone, and marginals = "gaussian" alone is the Laplace approximation with the VB correction.

Usage

inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init,
  grad = NULL,
  ...,
  vb = TRUE,
  marginals = c("skewnormal", "gaussian"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  silent = FALSE,
  control = list()
)

Arguments

logpost

A function logpost(theta, ...) returning the log-posterior density (up to a constant) at the named numeric vector theta, on the unconstrained scale. See the section on writing logpost.

init

A named numeric vector of starting values. Its length sets the number of parameters and its names label them; unnamed values are called theta[1], theta[2], ..., and a repeated name is numbered in the same way.

grad

Optional function grad(theta, ...) returning the gradient of logpost as a numeric vector. When NULL (the default), finite differences are used.

...

Further arguments passed to logpost and grad, such as the data. As in stats::optim() and stats::nlminb(), they come after the gradient, and the arguments after them (vb, marginals, verbose, silent, control) must be given by their full names, so data arguments cannot partially match them. The arguments before them can be matched, as in optim(): a data argument named g or gr would be taken as grad, so give it a longer name.

vb

Logical. Apply the VB mean correction? Default TRUE. It enters the log marginal likelihood, and the skew-normal means are checked against it (see summary.inla_vanilla()).

marginals

The marginal of each parameter: "skewnormal" (the default) fits a skew-normal to a scan of the log-posterior; "gaussian" uses the Gaussian marginal of the Laplace approximation, centred at the VB mean when vb = TRUE, with no scans. Abbreviations such as "skew" and "gauss" work too.

verbose

Logical. Print a full diagnostic of each stage under its progress line? Default FALSE. See the section on output.

silent

Logical. Print nothing at all, and muffle the warnings and messages raised during the fit? Default FALSE. The warnings are still recorded in fit$warnings. Cannot be combined with verbose = TRUE.

control

A list of tuning parameters; see the section on control.

Value

An object of class inla_vanilla, with methods for print(), summary(), plot() and sampling(). It is a list holding, among other things:

  • summary: the posterior summary table (mean, SD, quantiles, mode).

  • mode, cov: the Laplace mode and covariance.

  • mean_vb: the VB-corrected mean (the mode when vb = FALSE).

  • sn: the skew-normal parameters xi, omega and alpha per parameter (with alpha = 0 for Gaussian marginals).

  • vb, marginals, verbose, silent: the settings the fit used.

  • logml: the log marginal likelihood.

  • warnings: the messages of the warnings raised during the fit, as a character vector of plain text, each message once (empty when there were none). They are recorded whether or not silent is TRUE.

Writing logpost

The approximation works on an unconstrained scale: every parameter must be free to take any real value. Reparameterise anything constrained, for example a standard deviation \(\sigma > 0\) as \(\log\sigma\), a probability as its logit, or a correlation as its Fisher \(z\). Means and regression coefficients need no change.

Return -Inf wherever the density is zero or cannot be evaluated, such as outside the support or where a matrix is not positive definite (NA and NaN count the same). The scans and the VB nodes reach several posterior SDs from the mode, and an error raised there stops the fit.

logpost is then the log density of the parameters you pass. When a prior is stated on the natural scale, include the log-Jacobian of the transformation: with \(\vartheta = \log\sigma\) and a prior \(p(\sigma)\), the prior term is \(\log p(e^\vartheta) + \vartheta\). Leaving it out targets a different posterior, not a worse approximation of the same one, and nothing downstream can detect it.

The choice of parameterisation also sets the quality of the approximation, since each parameter gets its own skew-normal on the scale you choose. Scales on which the posterior is close to Gaussian (log standard deviations, Fisher-\(z\) correlations, logits) work best. Natural-scale or derived quantities are available through sampling(fit, fun = ...).

The log marginal likelihood is an estimate of \(\log p(y)\) only when logpost returns the full \(\log p(y, \vartheta)\), including every normalising constant of the likelihood and the prior. Otherwise it is off by the missing constants.

Accuracy

The skew-normal marginals capture skewness that the Laplace approximation misses, and they are accurate to the extent that a skew-normal fits each marginal (see the diagnostics in summary.inla_vanilla()). Like INLAvaan, each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, and the changing volume of the other parameters enters only to first order. When a parameter's spread depends strongly on another, poorly determined parameter, its marginal comes out too narrow, by a factor that vanishes as O(1/n). Examples are a regression coefficient or a mean when the noise SD is uncertain. For a normal mean with unknown variance the SD is about 11% too small at n = 12, 3% at n = 50, and under 1% at n = 200.

A skew-normal also cannot follow a tail heavier than a Gaussian's. In a structural equation model with 39 parameters and n = 75, the data could not keep two residual variances away from zero, so on the log scale their posteriors had a long, exponential left tail, set by the prior. Checked against MCMC, those two skew-normal marginals were less than half as wide as the posterior, with the 2.5% quantile about 2 posterior SDs too high; the other 37 were within 7% in SD. On the variance scale, where the tail near zero is compressed, the two were much closer: means 0.2 posterior SDs too high and SDs 10 to 15% too small. INLAvaan's marginals of this model are the same as inlavanilla's. The bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() flagged both, but its size does not say how far off a marginal is, and the tails check, which looks only 4 Laplace SDs out, missed them.

Gradients

grad is optional. Without it, derivatives come from finite differences of logpost, and the number of calls grows quickly with the number of parameters m. The mode and Hessian take about m^2 + 6m calls. The marginals take about m(n_grid + 2m + 5). The VB correction takes about (m + 1)(2m^2 + 1) calls per sweep, over a few sweeps, so it dominates beyond a handful of parameters: at m = 20 a fit makes on the order of 50,000 calls. With grad, the VB correction takes 2m^2 + 1 gradient calls per sweep instead, and the fit is faster and more accurate. For more than about 10 parameters, supply grad, or set vb = FALSE to skip the VB correction (and its term in the log marginal likelihood): the skew-normal marginals do not depend on it. marginals = "gaussian" saves the calls of the scans.

A supplied grad is checked against finite differences at init, and its Jacobian at the mode is checked for symmetry, with a warning if either check fails. Any R function works for logpost and grad, including compiled code (Rcpp, TMB, RTMB). For a TMB object, which minimises, pass function(x) -obj$fn(x) and function(x) -as.vector(obj$gr(x)), with init = obj$par; its repeated names (one per element of a parameter vector) are numbered, as beta[1], beta[2], and so on.

Control

control is a list with any of:

  • n_grid: number of grid points per skew-normal scan, spread over \(\pm 4\) posterior SDs (default 21).

  • log_threshold: grid points whose log-posterior falls more than this below the maximum are ignored in the skew-normal fit (default -6).

  • vb_maxit, vb_tol: iteration limit (default 25) and convergence tolerance in posterior SDs (default 1e-3) for the VB correction.

  • nlminb: a list of stats::nlminb() controls for the mode search. iter.max and eval.max default to 1000 and 2000, and trace = 1 prints its iterations.

Output

By default each stage prints one line as it finishes, with the time it took, and shows a progress bar while it runs for longer than half a second, or than the option cli.progress_show_after when it is set. In knitr or Quarto documents, where a bar cannot redraw in place, a larger cli.progress_show_after in the setup chunk keeps bars out of the output. Warnings, such as a mode that was not reached or a gradient that does not match logpost, are signalled as usual.

verbose = TRUE adds a full diagnostic of the fit, in grey lines under each stage. It reports what the fit computes anyway, with no further calls of logpost or grad:

  • Before the mode search: the parameters, where the derivatives come from, logpost at init, and for a supplied grad its largest relative discrepancy from finite differences there.

  • The mode: the message, iterations and evaluations of stats::nlminb(), and whether it was restarted with the parameters rescaled; the log-posterior and the whitened gradient at the mode; how the Hessian was taken (and, for a supplied grad, the asymmetry of its Jacobian); the largest posterior correlation and the smallest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix, which is near zero when some combination of the parameters is poorly identified; and the Laplace log marginal likelihood.

  • The VB correction: the largest step, in posterior SDs, at each fixed-point iteration, whether Anderson acceleration or the fallback optimiser was used, the largest shift, and the term it adds to the log marginal likelihood.

  • The marginals: the shape, NMAD, bend, tails and volume correction gamma1 of each parameter, with the values that summary.inla_vanilla() flags marked.

  • The calls of logpost and grad in each stage, and in all, with the total time.

For the iteration trace of stats::nlminb() itself, pass control = list(nlminb = list(trace = 1)).

silent = TRUE prints nothing, for simulations and other repeated fits: no progress bars and no stage lines, and every warning and message raised during the fit, including those of logpost and grad, is muffled. Errors are still raised. Output printed with cat() or print(), by logpost, grad or the trace of stats::nlminb(), is not captured.

Whatever the level, the warnings raised during the fit are recorded in fit$warnings, so that a simulation can check them afterwards.

References

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026a). Approximate Bayesian inference for structural equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (arXiv:2603.25690 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026b). Implementation and workflows for INLA-based approximate Bayesian structural equation modelling (arXiv:2604.00671 [stat.CO]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.00671

See also

sampling() for posterior draws and derived quantities, summary.inla_vanilla() for diagnostics.

Examples

# Normal data with unknown mean and standard deviation, on the scale
# (mu, log sigma)
set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(30, mean = 5, sd = 2)

logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  mu <- theta[["mu"]]
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) + # prior on mu
    dexp(sigma, rate = 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on sigma ...
    theta[["log_sigma"]] # ... and its Jacobian
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0), y = y)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [4ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.24σ [3ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [9ms]
fit
#> ── INLAvanilla ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 19ms ──
#> 2 parameters · skew-normal marginals · VB-corrected
#> 
#>             Mean     SD   2.5%    50%  97.5%   Mode
#> mu         5.159  0.327  4.517  5.159  5.800  5.159
#> log_sigma  0.616  0.129  0.377  0.610  0.885  0.599
#> 
#> Log marginal likelihood: -66.38

# The posterior of sigma itself, through the draws
sigma <- sampling(fit, fun = function(theta) exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]))
quantile(sigma, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>     2.5%      50%    97.5% 
#> 1.444354 1.832695 2.455869 

# A full diagnostic of each stage
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  y = y,
  verbose = TRUE
)
#> ℹ 2 parameters: mu and log_sigma
#>   Derivatives by finite differences of logpost
#>   logpost at init -481.47
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [1ms]
#>   nlminb: relative convergence (4), after 10 iterations (14 function and 26 gradient evaluations)
#>   logpost at the mode -65.06, whitened gradient 8.8e-08σ (warning above 0.01σ)
#>   Hessian by second differences of logpost: 6 calls, and 12 more to set the steps
#>   Posterior correlation matrix: largest correlation -0.0042 (mu, log_sigma), smallest eigenvalue 1
#>   Laplace log marginal likelihood -66.41
#>   63 logpost calls
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.24σ [2ms]
#>   Fixed-point steps, largest over the parameters (σ): 0.25, 0.0081, 2.4e-04
#>   Converged in 3 iterations, Anderson acceleration at 1 of them; no fallback
#>   Largest shift 0.24σ, for log_sigma
#>   KL term 0.03, giving a log marginal likelihood of -66.38
#>   81 logpost calls
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [7ms]
#>              Shape     NMAD     Bend  Tails    gamma1
#>   mu         -0.25  4.2e-05     0.13!    ok  -0.00014
#>   log_sigma   1.32   0.0076  5.5e-06     ok      0.13
#>   ! marks what summary() flags: NMAD above 0.05, bend above 0.1, heavy tails
#>   66 logpost calls
#> ℹ Done: 210 logpost calls in 20ms

# Nothing printed, as in a simulation; any warnings are kept in the fit
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  y = y,
  silent = TRUE
)
fit$warnings
#> character(0)
